title: A new industrial revolution
hook: Leo XIV says he took his name partly after Leo XIII, facing a new revolution in technology

segments.voice: Yesterday, migrants, and Francis's four verbs: welcome, protect, promote, integrate. Your line was four verbs. Which one did you manage to do? Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

Why Leo? A new pope, speaking to the cardinals who had just elected him, explained the name he'd chosen. Because of an earlier Leo, Leo the Thirteenth, who wrote Rerum Novarum, a letter on the condition of workers, at a time when factories and machines were remaking how people worked and lived. That was an industrial revolution. Today, the new pope, Leo the Fourteenth, says, the Church faces another one: a revolution in technology, artificial intelligence among it, raising new questions about human dignity, justice and work. A name chosen as a signal. Today is what he was pointing at.
screen: `A NEW POPE EXPLAINS HIS NAME.` → `LEO XIII AND THE FACTORIES.` → `ANOTHER REVOLUTION.`

segments.voice: First, the echo. Leo the Thirteenth described workers left isolated and helpless before hard employers and unchecked competition. He insisted that employers must not treat workers as slaves, or use people as things for profit. Leo the Fourteenth's point is that the same question has come back in new clothes. Second, the new machines. This time they don't only lift and weld. They sort, write, recommend and predict. They can help a doctor or a farmer. They can also replace a worker, track an employee's every minute, or decide what whole crowds of people see. Catholic social teaching doesn't treat technology as evil. It treats it as made by people, so it can be shaped by people, for people. Third, the measure. The tradition's test is simple to say and hard to keep: does this serve the human person, or does the person end up serving it? A good tool exists for people. When the order flips, something's gone wrong. Fourth, the old garden. In Genesis, God puts the first human in paradise "to dress it, and to keep it." Work and care, from the beginning. Not to be replaced, not to be used up, but to tend. That's the picture behind Leo the Fourteenth's signal: machines that help people tend the world, never people reduced to parts of a machine.
screen: `THE SAME QUESTION, NEW CLOTHES.` · `MACHINES THAT SORT, WRITE, PREDICT.` · `DOES IT SERVE THE PERSON?` · `TO DRESS IT, AND TO KEEP IT.` · then, large: `WORK AND CARE, FROM THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your own machines. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the screen you use most, the phone in your pocket or the computer on your desk. Think about yesterday. When did it serve you, and when did you end up serving it? A scroll that ate an hour. A notification that pulled you away from a face. Now pick one small change that puts the person first: phone in another room at dinner, a real voice instead of a text, one app silenced. If you pray, you can offer that choice to God. If you don't, simply decide it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
A new industrial revolution. Leo the Fourteenth's name for the change technology is bringing, and the reason he looked back to Leo the Thirteenth. Today's word.
Your line: people before machines. Today, make the one change you chose, and give the time it frees to a person. Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Catholic universities, dioceses and Vatican offices study the ethics of new technology and artificial intelligence in the light of social teaching, and Catholics discuss it in parish and workplace groups.

fork.setup: you manage a team. a new system could track every minute of your workers' day and cut their breaks. what does Catholic social teaching ask?
options: use it fully: efficiency is everything.
ask whether it serves the workers as people.
fork.reveal: the tradition doesn't reject technology. it asks one question: does this serve the human person, or does the person end up serving it?

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope worried about robots.
what it means: a pope naming a new revolution in technology and asking that it serve people, as Leo XIII asked of the factories.
what a scholar hears: a papal name chosen as a program, tying artificial intelligence to Rerum Novarum and the dignity of work.

notes: Leo XIV's explanation of his name (address to the College of Cardinals shortly after his election): mainly because Leo XIII in Rerum Novarum addressed the social question in the first great industrial revolution, and today the Church offers its social teaching in response to another industrial revolution and developments in artificial intelligence. Paraphrased; confirm wording, and that 'opened modern Catholic social teaching' is a fair description of Rerum Novarum.
Conditions of workers in Leo XIII's time are described generally; confirm.
Examples of technology's uses (helping a doctor, tracking employees) are illustrations, not from the address.
